description: Test your knowledge of Front & Medial side of thigh.

cards.text: What are the primary actions of iliopsoas, and what is the clinical significance of a psoas abscess?
cards.answer: Iliopsoas is the primary hip flexor. A psoas abscess results from TB of lumbar spine where pus tracks through the psoas sheath, presenting as a fluctuant swelling in the femoral triangle (cold abscess without fever).

tip.tip: Remember: TB spine → tracks down psoas sheath → cold swelling in femoral triangle. Think tuberculosis, not acute infection.

cards.text: Which head of quadriceps femoris is bi-articular, and what are its unique actions?
cards.answer: Rectus femoris is the only bi-articular head of quadriceps, originating from AIIS and acetabular rim. It performs both hip flexion and knee extension.

tip.tip: Rectus = "Right down the middle" + RECtus = Rectus = flexes at hip too. Only quadriceps head that crosses both joints.

cards.text: What is the nerve supply of the quadriceps femoris, and what is the earliest clinical sign of disuse after knee injury?
cards.answer: Femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) supplies all four heads. Quadriceps wasting is the earliest sign of disuse; vastus medialis wasting specifically increases risk of patellar subluxation.

tip.tip: Quadriceps wasting = first sign. VMO (vastus medialis obliquus) loss = patellar instability. Watch the medial quad first.

cards.text: Name the contents of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial.
cards.answer: Femoral Nerve (L2–L4), Artery (central), Vein (medial to artery), Empty space — mnemonic NAVEL.

tip.tip: NAVEL: N-A-V-E-L (lateral to medial). Nerve is lateral, vein medial to artery. Empty space is medial.

cards.text: What is the adductor hiatus, and why is it clinically important?
cards.answer: The adductor hiatus is an opening near the adductor tubercle of the femur in adductor magnus. It allows the femoral vessels to pass through into the popliteal fossa, transitioning them to popliteal vessels.

tip.tip: Hiatus = hole. Femoral vessels pass THROUGH adductor magnus hiatus to become popliteal vessels. Critical for vascular continuity.

cards.text: Which nerve supplies the medial (adductor) compartment of the thigh, and what is one clinical application of this anatomy?
cards.answer: Obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) supplies the adductor group. By Hilton's law, hip joint pain can be referred to the medial knee via the obturator nerve's articular branch.

tip.tip: Obturator nerve = adductors. Hip pain → medial knee pain (Hilton's law). Think shared innervation patterns.

cards.text: Name the longest muscle in the body and describe its path and insertion.
cards.answer: Sartorius is the longest muscle. It originates at ASIS and courses obliquely medially across the thigh to insert on the upper medial tibia as part of the pes anserinus (with gracilis and semitendinosus).

tip.tip: Sartorius = "tailor's muscle" (sitting cross-legged pose). Long diagonal course = ASIS to medial tibia. Pes anserinus = "goose foot."

cards.text: Why is vastus medialis obliquus (VMO) particularly important clinically, and what happens when it atrophies?
cards.answer: VMO, with its oblique fiber orientation, actively prevents lateral patellar subluxation and maintains proper patellar tracking. VMO wasting leads to loss of this medial support and increased risk of patellar subluxation.

tip.tip: VMO = patella's medial guard. No VMO = patellar drift lateral. First quad muscle to atrophy, last to recover — rehab priority.
